question: Describe a time when you brought different perspectives together to solve a problem. What types of different perspectives were represented? How did you seek out different points of view? What was the outcome? Were there any key learnings from this experience? Knowing what you know now, would you have done anything different?
competency: Are Right, A Lot (seeking truth through diverse viewpoints)

raiseTranscript.text: On a feature launch, the PM wanted to prioritize speed while the designer pushed for accessibility. I asked both to join a 30-minute sync, pulled in the support ticket data I had, and we landed on a phased rollout that met the deadline and fixed the main a11y gaps.
How did you decide who to include?
I checked the ticket queue and asked the on-call engineer what broke last time we rushed something.
I would have written down the decision criteria before the meeting so the trade-off was clearer.

raiseNotes: Q: Describe a time when you brought different perspectives together...
Story: PM vs designer on speed vs a11y; used support data and on-call input
Sought views by checking tickets and asking on-call engineer
Outcome: phased rollout met deadline and fixed main gaps
Quote: 'I asked both to join a 30-minute sync'
Follow-up: Would change by writing decision criteria first
junior.raiseFeedback: The candidate described a concrete, scoped disagreement between PM and designer and used ticket data plus an on-call engineer to surface facts. They sought input by directly checking existing data rather than assuming consensus. The outcome was a practical compromise that shipped on time. They reflected on the need for explicit decision criteria, showing coachability. This meets the bar for a junior role where local ownership and learning from feedback are the focus. The main strength is the willingness to pull in the right person without overstepping scope.

lowerTranscript.text: I had a disagreement with a teammate about the color of a button. I talked to my manager and we decided to keep the original color.
What other perspectives did you seek?
Just my manager. The designer was busy so I didn't want to bother them.

lowerNotes: Q: Describe a time when you brought different perspectives together...
Story: Button color disagreement resolved by manager
Sought views: only manager, avoided designer
Outcome: kept original color
Quote: 'The designer was busy so I didn't want to bother them'
Follow-up: No evidence of data or broader input
junior.lowerFeedback: The example stayed at a trivial UI detail and only involved the manager, showing no attempt to gather real differing views. The candidate avoided the designer explicitly rather than seeking their input. No data or customer signal was referenced. Reflection was absent. This lowers the bar for Are Right, A Lot at the junior level because even early-career hires should show basic curiosity about other viewpoints on their own work.

raiseTranscript.text: Two teams disagreed on whether to build a shared service or keep separate implementations. I scheduled 1:1s with the leads, pulled usage metrics from both systems, and ran a joint working session that produced a short decision doc.
One lead still wanted to go alone, so I asked them to own the migration cost estimate and present it back to the group.
We adopted the shared path and the other team reduced their on-call load by 40 percent.

raiseNotes: Q: Describe a time when you brought different perspectives together...
Story: Two teams on shared service vs separate; used metrics and joint session
Sought views via 1:1s and asked resistant lead to own cost estimate
Outcome: shared path adopted, 40% on-call reduction
Quote: 'I asked them to own the migration cost estimate'
Follow-up: Would run the cost exercise earlier to shorten debate
senior.raiseFeedback: The candidate identified a cross-team conflict and used usage metrics plus structured 1:1s to surface facts before a group discussion. They handled resistance by assigning the dissenting lead a concrete analysis task rather than arguing. The result delivered measurable operational relief. Reflection included a specific process improvement for next time. This raises the bar for a senior because it shows influence across teams and use of data to reach the right technical decision.

lowerTranscript.text: I invited everyone to a big meeting and we talked until we agreed on the design.
I summarized what people said in the meeting.

lowerNotes: Q: Describe a time when you brought different perspectives together...
Story: Large meeting to reach design agreement
Sought views: open invitation and discussion
Outcome: agreement reached
Quote: 'I summarized what people said in the meeting'
Follow-up: No metrics or targeted outreach shown
senior.lowerFeedback: The approach relied on a single large meeting without prior data or targeted outreach, which rarely surfaces the strongest arguments. No attempt was made to quantify trade-offs or give dissenters ownership of analysis. The outcome is stated as agreement without evidence it was the right one. This lowers the bar for a senior because Are Right, A Lot at this level requires deliberate collection of evidence across teams, not just facilitation.

raiseTranscript.text: My team and the platform team had opposing priorities on a reliability investment. I asked each team to list their top three risks with data, then facilitated a joint review where we ranked them together and assigned owners.
How did you develop your people through this?
I had the two tech leads co-own the final recommendation and present it to leadership.

raiseNotes: Q: Describe a time when you brought different perspectives together...
Story: Team vs platform on reliability; used risk lists and joint ranking
Sought views by requiring data-backed risks from each side
Outcome: ranked risks and assigned owners
Quote: 'I had the two tech leads co-own the final recommendation'
Follow-up: Used the process to grow leads by giving them visibility
manager.raiseFeedback: The manager created a structured process that forced both teams to surface data rather than opinions and then gave leads joint ownership of the output. This built capability in the team while reaching a decision aligned with actual risk. The approach shows leverage through others instead of the manager deciding alone. Reflection is implicit in the repeatable method. This raises the bar for a manager because it demonstrates developing people while owning team-level outcomes.

lowerTranscript.text: I listened to both sides and made the call that felt fairest.
Did you ask your reports to gather data?
No, I wanted to keep it quick so the teams could move on.

lowerNotes: Q: Describe a time when you brought different perspectives together...
Story: Listened to both sides and decided
Sought views: direct listening only
Outcome: fairest call made
Quote: 'I wanted to keep it quick so the teams could move on'
Follow-up: No development of reports or data requirement
manager.lowerFeedback: The manager defaulted to personal judgment without requiring data or involving reports in the analysis. Speed was prioritized over building team capability. No evidence that the decision was actually right, only that it felt fair. This lowers the bar for a manager role because Are Right, A Lot requires creating mechanisms that let the team reach better answers over time.

raiseTranscript.text: Engineering and finance disagreed on whether to sunset a low-margin product line. I commissioned a small cross-functional group with P&L data, customer interviews, and competitive analysis, then had them present three scenarios to the ELT.
We exited the line, freed 12 engineers, and the retained customers showed higher NPS within two quarters.

raiseNotes: Q: Describe a time when you brought different perspectives together...
Story: Eng vs finance on product sunsetting; commissioned data-driven group
Sought views via P&L, customer interviews, competitive analysis
Outcome: exit freed 12 engineers, NPS improved
Quote: 'had them present three scenarios to the ELT'
Follow-up: Would have included regulatory view earlier
exec.raiseFeedback: The executive framed a high-stakes, ambiguous business decision and created a cross-functional fact-finding team with clear deliverables rather than mediating opinions. Multiple data sources including customer and competitive signals were required. The outcome produced both resource leverage and measurable customer improvement. The candidate noted a missing perspective for future decisions. This raises the bar at the exec level because it shows strategic judgment and the ability to drive org-level clarity through structured debate.

lowerTranscript.text: I held an offsite with the two VPs and we aligned on the direction.
What external data informed the decision?
The VPs brought their teams' views.

lowerNotes: Q: Describe a time when you brought different perspectives together...
Story: Offsite with two VPs to align
Sought views: internal VP perspectives only
Outcome: alignment reached
Quote: 'The VPs brought their teams' views'
Follow-up: No external or customer data referenced
exec.lowerFeedback: The approach stayed inside the company and relied on two VPs negotiating rather than testing assumptions against market or customer reality. No mechanism was created to surface contradictory evidence. The result is stated as alignment without proof it was the strategically correct choice. This lowers the bar for an exec because Are Right, A Lot at this level demands forcing functions that incorporate external signals before committing resources.

diagnostic.junior: Used existing tickets to ground discussion
diagnostic.senior: Pulled cross-team usage metrics before meeting
diagnostic.manager: Required each team to list risks with data
diagnostic.exec: Commissioned P&L, customer interviews, competitive analysis

diagnostic.senior: Assigned resistant lead the cost estimate task
diagnostic.manager: Gave tech leads joint ownership of recommendation
diagnostic.exec: Structured three scenarios for ELT review

diagnostic.junior: Would write decision criteria upfront next time
diagnostic.manager: Process now used to develop leads
